stem: A good is scarce, in the economic sense, when
option_a: everyone already has as much as they want
option_b: more of it is wanted than is freely available at a zero price
option_c: it cannot be produced by labour
explanation: Scarcity means wants exceed availability at a zero price, so the good has an opportunity cost. A free good does not.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: A production possibility frontier shows
option_a: the prices consumers are willing to pay
option_b: only the goods that are imported
option_c: the maximum combinations of two goods that can be produced when resources are fully and efficiently employed
option_d: combinations that are always inside the country's budget
explanation: The PPF is a boundary of maximum output of two goods, given resources and technology, with full employment of those resources.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: Opportunity cost is
option_a: the sum of money spent on every alternative
option_b: a cost that is always zero in a mixed economy
option_c: the next best alternative given up when a choice is made
option_d: the total output of the economy
explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the best forgone alternative, not every alternative added together.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: The three basic choices for an economy are
option_a: what to consume, how to save, and for whom to lend abroad only
option_b: what to tax, how to vote, and for whom to export only
option_c: what the central bank prints, how banks advertise, and for whom interest is paid
option_d: what to produce, how to produce, and for whom to produce
explanation: Scarcity forces every economy to decide what is produced, which methods are used, and who receives the output.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: Which contrast between microeconomics and macroeconomics is correct?
option_a: Microeconomics studies inflation only; macroeconomics studies one firm only
option_b: Macroeconomics ignores national income and studies only one household
option_c: Microeconomics studies individual markets; macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole
option_d: Both study only the foreign-exchange market
explanation: Microeconomics looks at households, firms and particular markets. Macroeconomics looks at aggregates such as national income, inflation and unemployment.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: Which statement best defines economics as it is used in this syllabus?
option_a: The study of how banks set every price in a modern economy
option_b: The study of unlimited resources and limited human wants
option_c: The recording of government tax revenue only
option_d: The study of how scarce resources are allocated among competing uses
explanation: Economics starts from scarcity: wants exceed the resources available, so choice is unavoidable.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: A point inside the production possibility frontier of Westford indicates
option_a: unemployment or inefficient use of existing resources
option_b: a combination that is impossible with current resources
explanation: Points inside the frontier are attainable but inefficient. Points on the frontier are efficient. Points outside are unattainable with current resources.

stem: A point outside the current production possibility frontier is
option_a: the equilibrium of demand and supply
option_b: proof that the economy is in recession
option_c: always preferred by consumers to a point on the frontier
option_d: unattainable with present resources and technology
explanation: The frontier is the maximum. Output beyond it needs more resources or better technology.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: Air at the roadside in Port Clare is freely available and nobody has to give anything up to breathe it. In economics this air is best treated as
option_a: a public good that must be rationed by price
option_b: a factor of production called enterprise
explanation: A free good is not scarce. An economic good requires a sacrifice of something else.

stem: The government of St Brice spends a given budget on a new clinic and therefore postpones a harbour repair. The opportunity cost of the clinic is
option_a: the wages of nurses in other countries
option_b: the sum of every project the government has ever discussed
option_c: zero, because the clinic is useful
option_d: the harbour repair that was given up
explanation: The opportunity cost of a choice is the next best alternative forgone, here the harbour repair.

stem: Which statement is normative?
option_a: Harbour Cay produced 20 000 tonnes of fish last year in this classroom example
option_b: The government of Harbour Cay ought to subsidise school meals
option_c: The marginal propensity to consume is the change in consumption divided by the change in income
option_d: A price ceiling set below equilibrium causes a shortage
explanation: A normative statement contains a value judgement such as 'ought'. The other statements are positive: they can be tested.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: Which statement is positive?
option_a: The government must always prefer equality to growth
option_b: The minimum wage is unfair and should be abolished
option_c: Tourism is a better industry than farming
option_d: A rise in the minimum wage in a competitive labour market reduces the quantity of labour demanded
explanation: A positive statement is a testable claim. Saying a policy is unfair, better, or must be preferred is normative.

stem: A market is in equilibrium when
option_a: producers hold unwanted stocks that keep growing
option_c: the government fixes a price below the market-clearing price
explanation: Equilibrium is the price at which planned purchases equal planned sales, so there is no tendency for the price to change.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: A specific tax is levied on producers. Which statement is correct?
option_a: The tax shifts demand to the right
option_b: Buyers always pay the entire tax, whatever the elasticities
option_c: Sellers always pay the entire tax, whatever the elasticities
option_d: The price buyers pay rises and the price sellers keep falls, and the more inelastic side of the market bears more of the tax
explanation: The tax drives a wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive. Incidence depends on relative elasticities: the less elastic side bears more.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: A minimum price is set above equilibrium. The result is
option_a: no change, because a floor above equilibrium does not bind
option_d: an increase in quantity demanded above quantity supplied
explanation: A price floor above equilibrium is binding. At that higher price, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: A price ceiling is set above the equilibrium price. The ceiling
option_a: is non-binding and the market stays at the equilibrium price
option_c: forces the price down to zero
explanation: A maximum price above the price that the market would set does not constrain buyers and sellers.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: A price ceiling is set below the equilibrium price. The result is
option_a: a quantity traded equal to quantity demanded
option_c: a shortage, and the quantity traded is the quantity supplied
option_d: no effect, because a ceiling below equilibrium is non-binding
explanation: A maximum price below equilibrium is binding. Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, and trade is limited by the smaller amount, which is quantity supplied.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: At the current price there is a shortage. In a free market
option_a: price falls until a larger shortage appears
option_b: price rises until quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
option_d: demand must shift left by law
explanation: A shortage means buyers bid the price up. The higher price reduces quantity demanded and raises quantity supplied.

stem: At the current price, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded. In a free market the price will
option_a: stay the same because a surplus is an equilibrium
explanation: A surplus puts downward pressure on price. As price falls, quantity demanded rises and quantity supplied falls until the surplus disappears.

stem: Both the demand curve and the supply curve of cement shift right. Which conclusion is certain?

explanation: Each shift raises quantity, so quantity rises. Demand alone would raise price and supply alone would lower it, so the price change depends on which shift is larger.

explanation: When demand is perfectly inelastic, quantity does not fall and buyers pay the whole tax. If supply were perfectly inelastic, sellers would bear the whole tax.

stem: A limitation of cardinal marginal-utility theory is that
option_a: satisfaction cannot in practice be measured in objective utility units
option_b: it denies that consumers respond to prices
option_c: it assumes diminishing marginal utility, which no textbook uses
option_d: it cannot be stated as an equation
explanation: The cardinal approach treats utility as measurable in utils. In practice utility is not cardinally measurable, which is why the ordinal indifference-curve approach is used.

stem: An indifference curve shows
option_b: the market demand of all consumers added together
option_c: combinations of two goods that give the consumer the same satisfaction
option_d: the cost of producing two goods
explanation: Each indifference curve is a set of bundles among which the consumer is indifferent. A budget line shows what the consumer can afford.

stem: Consumer equilibrium in cardinal utility theory occurs when
option_a: marginal utility is rising for every good
option_c: the consumer buys only the cheapest good, whatever its marginal utility
option_d: the marginal utility per dollar is equal for every good bought, and income is spent
explanation: The equi-marginal condition is MUa/Pa = MUb/Pb, with the budget exhausted.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: Marginal utility is
option_a: the extra satisfaction from consuming one more unit
option_b: always rising as more units are consumed
option_c: satisfaction from all units consumed, added together
option_d: total utility divided by price only when price is zero
explanation: Marginal utility is the change in total utility from one extra unit. Total utility is the sum of satisfaction from all units.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: Ordinal consumer equilibrium is at the point where
option_a: two indifference curves cross the budget line at different slopes
option_c: the budget line is tangent to an indifference curve
option_d: the consumer is on the lowest indifference curve that cuts the budget line twice
explanation: Tangency means the marginal rate of substitution equals the price ratio, and the consumer reaches the highest affordable indifference curve.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: The law of diminishing marginal utility states that, beyond some point,
option_a: marginal utility rises with every extra unit
option_b: extra units of a good add less satisfaction than the previous unit, other things equal
option_d: total utility falls as soon as consumption begins
explanation: Diminishing marginal utility means successive units yield less additional satisfaction, holding other things constant.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: The slope of the budget line, in absolute value, equals
option_b: the price of the good on the horizontal axis divided by the price of the good on the vertical axis
explanation: If good X is on the horizontal axis, the budget line has slope minus Px/Py. Income changes shift the line; a relative-price change rotates it.

stem: Utility means
option_c: the price printed on the good
option_d: the satisfaction a consumer obtains from a good or service
explanation: Utility is satisfaction. It is not the same thing as price or cost.

stem: Which property of a standard indifference map is correct?
option_a: Every curve is concave to the origin
option_b: Curves further from the origin represent higher satisfaction, and two curves do not cross
option_c: Curves slope upwards because both goods are desirable
option_d: Curves cross at the consumer's equilibrium
explanation: More of both goods is preferred, so higher curves are better. Crossing would imply inconsistent rankings. Standard curves are convex to the origin.

stem: A consumer buys goods A and B. The marginal utility of A divided by its price is greater than the marginal utility of B divided by its price. To move toward equilibrium the consumer should
option_a: buy more B and less A
option_b: buy more A and less B
option_c: stop buying A because its marginal utility is too high
option_d: buy more of both in the same proportion
explanation: Equilibrium requires MUa/Pa = MUb/Pb. If MUa/Pa is higher, the last dollar spent on A yields more utility, so the consumer gains by switching spending toward A.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

explanation: When marginal utility is positive, total utility rises. If marginal utility is falling, total utility rises more slowly. Total utility is maximised when marginal utility is zero.

stem: In Golden Vale, the price of painted tiles rises from EC$16 to EC$20 and quantity demanded changes from 125 to 75. Total revenue changes from EC$2000 to EC$1500. Measured by the simple percentage method, demand over this range is

stem: In Port Clare, the price of bus fares rises from EC$20 to EC$24 and quantity demanded changes from 90 to 81. Total revenue changes from EC$1800 to EC$1944. Measured by the simple percentage method, demand over this range is
option_a: price inelastic, and the higher price increases total revenue
option_b: price inelastic, and the price change has the opposite total-revenue effect from the one observed
option_c: perfectly inelastic, so quantity demanded does not change
option_d: unit elastic, so total revenue must stay exactly the same
explanation: Simple PED is 0.5, so demand is price inelastic. Total revenue moves from EC$1800 to EC$1944, so it rises.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: In St Brice, the price of craft baskets rises from EC$10 to EC$14 and quantity demanded changes from 100 to 50. Total revenue changes from EC$1000 to EC$700. Measured by the simple percentage method, demand over this range is
option_a: perfectly inelastic, so quantity demanded does not change
option_b: price elastic, and the higher price reduces total revenue
option_c: unit elastic, so total revenue must stay exactly the same
option_d: price inelastic, and the price change has the opposite total-revenue effect from the one observed
explanation: Simple PED is 1.25, so demand is price elastic. Total revenue moves from EC$1000 to EC$700, so it falls.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: In Westford, the price of room nights falls from EC$30 to EC$24 and quantity demanded changes from 40 to 56. Total revenue changes from EC$1200 to EC$1344. Measured by the simple percentage method, demand over this range is
option_a: price elastic, and the lower price increases total revenue
option_b: price inelastic, and the price change has the opposite total-revenue effect from the one observed
option_c: perfectly inelastic, so quantity demanded does not change
option_d: unit elastic, so total revenue must stay exactly the same
explanation: Simple PED is 2, so demand is price elastic. Total revenue moves from EC$1200 to EC$1344, so it rises.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: In the short run, the supply curve of a perfectly competitive firm is
option_a: its marginal-cost curve above average variable cost
option_c: a vertical line at zero output whatever the price
option_d: its marginal-cost curve below average variable cost
explanation: The firm supplies where price equals marginal cost, but only if price covers average variable cost. Below that, it shuts down.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: Normal profit is
option_a: the same thing as supernormal profit
option_c: the minimum return that keeps the entrepreneur in the industry, and it counts as zero economic profit
option_d: any revenue above total cost, including opportunity cost
explanation: Normal profit covers the opportunity cost of enterprise and is included in economic cost. Economic profit is then zero. Supernormal profit is positive economic profit.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: Producer surplus is
option_a: the area above the demand curve
option_c: the amount sellers receive above the minimum they would have accepted
explanation: Producer surplus is the gap between the price received and the marginal cost, or the minimum acceptable price, summed over the units sold.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: The law of diminishing returns applies when
option_a: average cost falls as the scale of the firm increases
option_b: at least one factor is fixed and extra units of a variable factor eventually add less output
option_c: demand for the product is inelastic
option_d: all factors are variable in the long run
explanation: Diminishing returns is a short-run idea: one factor is fixed. Economies of scale are a long-run idea, when all factors can change.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: Which matching of a factor of production to its reward is correct?
option_a: Enterprise earns interest and capital earns profit only
option_b: Land earns rent, labour earns wages, capital earns interest, and enterprise earns profit
option_c: Capital earns rent and land earns profit only
option_d: Land earns wages and labour earns rent
explanation: The factor rewards used in this syllabus are rent, wages, interest and profit.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: A firm reports a positive accounting profit, but that profit is only just enough to cover the entrepreneur's next best earnings. Economic profit is
option_c: negative and larger than the accounting profit in magnitude
explanation: Accounting profit ignores some opportunity costs. Once the entrepreneur's alternative earnings are treated as a cost, economic profit is zero. That is normal profit.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: A firm should shut down in the short run if price is
option_a: equal to marginal cost and above average variable cost
option_b: below average total cost but above average variable cost
explanation: If price is below average variable cost, producing adds to losses. If price covers average variable cost but not total cost, the firm still produces in the short run because it covers variable cost and part of fixed cost.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: A per-unit subsidy is paid to producers of solar lamps. The supply curve
option_a: does not move, because subsidies affect demand only
option_d: shifts right, or downward by the amount of the subsidy
explanation: A producer subsidy lowers the cost of supplying each unit, so firms offer more at each price.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: A rise in the market price of fish, with cost conditions unchanged, causes
option_c: a movement up along the supply curve
explanation: Own-price changes cause movements along supply. Cost, technology, taxes and the number of firms shift supply.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: Marginal product is positive but falling. Total product is
explanation: Total product rises while marginal product is positive. It rises more slowly when marginal product is falling. Total product is maximised when marginal product is zero.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: Which change shifts the supply curve of yams to the left?
option_a: A good harvest caused by better weather
option_b: A fall in the price of fertiliser
option_c: A rise in the wages of farm workers, with no change in yam technology
explanation: Higher input costs reduce supply. Better weather, cheaper inputs and better technology increase supply.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: A Pigouvian tax on a negative production externality should, in principle, be set equal to
option_a: the entire price of the good
option_b: the marginal external cost at the socially efficient output
option_d: zero, because taxes cannot change output
explanation: A tax equal to marginal external cost makes the firm face marginal social cost, so it chooses the smaller socially efficient output.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: An argument against government intervention is that
option_a: administrative costs and political pressure can make the cure worse than the market failure
explanation: Intervention is not automatically better than the market. The benefits of a policy have to be compared with its costs and with the risk of government failure.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: Government failure occurs when
option_a: a Pigouvian tax equals marginal external cost
option_c: intervention leaves society worse off than the market outcome it tried to correct, or wastes resources
explanation: Governments can misjudge the size of an externality, favour interest groups, or impose administrative costs larger than the benefit.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: Regulation that simply bans pollution above a limit, compared with a tax,
option_a: can hit a quantity target but may not minimise the cost of doing so if firms face different abatement costs
option_b: is the same instrument as a producer subsidy
option_c: always costs less than a tax for every firm
explanation: A uniform quota ignores which firms can cut pollution more cheaply. A tax or permit market gives those firms a stronger reason to cut more.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: Tradable pollution permits
option_a: are a form of public good provided free to polluters with no cap
option_b: cap the total quantity of pollution and let firms buy and sell the right to emit
option_c: force every firm to emit the same amount whatever the cost
option_d: set no limit on total pollution
explanation: The cap fixes the total externality. Trade lets firms that can cut emissions cheaply sell permits to firms that cannot, which reduces the cost of meeting the cap.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: A natural monopoly, with falling average cost over the whole market, is sometimes regulated rather than broken up because
option_a: one firm can produce the whole output at a lower average cost than several firms
option_b: competition always lowers average cost in this case
option_c: marginal cost is above average cost
explanation: When average cost is still falling at market demand, splitting the firm raises cost. Regulation may then be used to limit the monopoly price.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: A subsidy is a suitable market-based response to
option_a: a pure monopoly, if the aim is to raise price
option_b: a positive externality that causes under-consumption or under-production
option_c: a shortage caused by a price ceiling, if the aim is to lower supply
option_d: a negative externality that causes over-production, if the aim is to raise output further
explanation: A subsidy lowers the private cost or price and increases quantity, which can close the gap created by a positive externality.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: Competition policy is used to
option_a: force every industry to become a monopoly
option_b: ban all advertising of differentiated products
option_c: restrict abuse of monopoly power and anti-competitive agreements
option_d: set price equal to average fixed cost
explanation: Laws against cartels, mergers that harm competition, and abuse of a dominant position are meant to move price and output closer to the competitive outcome.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: Compulsory labelling of the health risk on a demerit good is an intervention aimed at
explanation: If over-consumption comes from consumers not knowing the risk, information can change demand without banning the good.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: Governments often provide street lighting directly because
option_a: it is a private good with no free riders
option_c: it is a public good and the market would under-provide it
option_d: marginal cost is always above willingness to pay
explanation: Non-excludability and non-rivalry make voluntary payment unreliable, so public provision or public finance is a standard remedy.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: Providing a merit good free at the point of use is intended to
option_a: raise consumption toward the socially desirable level
option_c: turn the good into a demerit good
explanation: A zero price removes the private cost barrier. That can be justified when information failure or external benefits mean the market quantity is too low, though it has a cost in taxation and possible over-use.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: Which intervention directly targets a negative consumption externality of cigarettes?
option_a: A subsidy that lowers the price
option_b: A price ceiling that creates a shortage and raises consumption
option_c: A specific tax that raises the price buyers pay
option_d: Free provision of cigarettes as if they were a public good
explanation: A tax reduces quantity demanded. A subsidy or free provision would increase consumption, which is the wrong direction for a demerit good.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: Which is a possible cost of using a tax to correct an externality?
option_a: Taxes cannot be levied on producers
option_b: If the tax is much larger than the marginal external cost, output falls below the social optimum
option_c: The tax removes private costs as well as external costs from the firm's accounts
option_d: A correctly set tax always increases the externality
explanation: Too large a tax over-corrects. The firm then produces less than the output at which marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: A demerit good is
option_a: a good with a positive consumption externality only
option_c: a good that the free market over-consumes relative to the socially desirable level
explanation: Demerit goods, such as cigarettes in the usual example, are over-consumed because consumers ignore harm to themselves or others, or lack information.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: A merit good is
option_b: a good that the free market under-consumes relative to the socially desirable level, often because of poor information or a positive externality
option_d: a good that is always non-excludable
explanation: Merit goods, such as preventive health care or basic education in the usual examples, are under-consumed if left only to private decisions. They can still be private goods.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: A negative production externality means
option_a: the good is a public good
option_b: marginal social benefit is above marginal private benefit
option_c: marginal social cost is below marginal private cost, and the market produces too little
option_d: marginal social cost is above marginal private cost, and the free market produces too much
explanation: The firm ignores costs imposed on others, so MSC = MPC + external cost. Private equilibrium output is higher than the social optimum.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: A positive consumption externality means
option_a: the good must be a demerit good
option_b: marginal social cost exceeds marginal private cost
option_d: marginal social benefit exceeds marginal private benefit, and the free market consumes too little
explanation: Others gain from this consumption, but the buyer counts only private benefit, so too little is consumed.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: A pure private good is
option_b: non-rival and excludable only if it is a public good
explanation: One person's consumption of a private good reduces what is left for others, and non-payers can be kept from using it.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: A pure public good is
option_d: excludable and always sold by a monopolist
explanation: Non-rival means one person's use does not reduce another's. Non-excludable means non-payers cannot be kept out. Street lighting is the usual example.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: An allocation is Pareto efficient when
option_a: nobody can be made better off without making someone else worse off
option_b: one person can gain without any cost to anyone else, and that change has not yet been made
explanation: Pareto efficiency means all mutually beneficial changes have already been exhausted. It does not mean incomes are equal.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: Information failure causes market failure when
option_a: the good is a free good
option_b: buyers or sellers lack information and so consume or produce the wrong amount
explanation: If consumers do not know the benefits of a merit good, or the harm of a demerit good, their choices are not the efficient ones.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: Market failure means that
option_a: the free market does not achieve an efficient allocation of resources
option_c: the market price is above zero
explanation: Failure is judged against efficiency, especially allocative efficiency, not against the mere existence of a price.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: Missing markets, as a cause of market failure, means
option_b: the stock exchange has closed for a holiday

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: An open-access fishery, where anyone may fish and one boat's catch reduces the stock, is
option_a: rival but non-excludable, so it tends to be overused
option_b: a pure private good, because a licence is always required
option_c: a pure public good, because the fish are non-rival
explanation: Fish taken by one boat are not available to others, so the resource is rival. If nobody can be excluded, fishers ignore the cost they impose on others and overfish. That is not a pure public good.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: Education can be excludable and rival in a classroom, yet still be treated as a merit good. That shows
option_b: rivalry and exclusion are the same thing
option_c: education cannot have a positive externality
option_d: a merit good need not be a public good
explanation: Public goods are defined by non-rivalry and non-exclusion. Merit goods are defined by under-consumption. A good can be one without being the other.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: Monopoly power is a source of market failure because
option_a: price is set above marginal cost, so too little is produced
option_b: free entry removes every barrier at once
option_d: the firm must produce at minimum average cost
explanation: The output where MR = MC is smaller than the output where P = MC. That under-production is allocatively inefficient.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: Smoke from a factory harms nearby residents and the firm does not pay them. This is
explanation: The cost falls on third parties during production and is not in the firm's private cost. Output is likely to be too high.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: The free-rider problem of a public good arises because
option_a: the government always over-provides private goods
option_b: marginal cost is above average cost
option_c: people can benefit without paying, so the market under-provides the good
option_d: the good is rival, so one user blocks every other user
explanation: If exclusion is impossible, each person waits for someone else to pay. Private firms then cannot cover costs from voluntary payments.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: The socially efficient output of a good with an external cost is where
option_a: marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost
option_b: marginal private cost equals marginal private benefit, ignoring the external cost
option_c: price is below marginal social cost by as much as possible
option_d: output is zero in every case
explanation: Efficiency requires all benefits and costs, including external ones, to be balanced at the margin. The private market equates only private benefit and private cost.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

option_a: the whole group of firms selling a product
option_c: a unit that employs factors to produce goods or services for sale
explanation: A firm produces for sale. An industry is the group of firms producing a particular product.

stem: A four-firm concentration ratio of 90 percent means
option_b: each of four firms has a 90 percent share
option_c: the largest four firms supply 90 percent of the market
explanation: CR4 is the sum of the market shares of the four largest firms. A high ratio means the industry is concentrated.

stem: A limitation of concentration ratios is that they
option_b: do not by themselves show barriers to entry, contestability or how firms actually behave
option_d: prove that price equals marginal cost
explanation: A high share can still be consistent with competitive pressure if entry is easy. Concentration is a structural clue, not a full measure of performance.

stem: A market is contestable when
option_b: entry and exit are easy and sunk costs are low, so even a few firms may behave competitively
option_c: one firm owns an essential resource that cannot be duplicated
explanation: The threat of hit-and-run entry can discipline incumbents if leaving does not sacrifice large sunk costs.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: A perfectly competitive firm is a price taker, so
option_a: marginal revenue is below average revenue
option_b: price equals average revenue and marginal revenue
option_c: the firm sets the market price on its own
option_d: average revenue falls as it sells more
explanation: The firm can sell any quantity at the market price, so the demand it faces is horizontal and P = AR = MR.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: A profit-maximising monopolist chooses the output where
option_a: marginal cost equals average revenue, always
option_c: price equals minimum average cost, by law
option_d: marginal revenue equals marginal cost, and then charges the price on the demand curve
explanation: The output rule is MR = MC for any profit-maximising firm. The monopolist reads the price from demand, so price exceeds marginal cost.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

option_a: price is greater than marginal cost
option_c: it must produce at minimum average cost
option_d: it earns only normal profit by definition
explanation: P > MC means consumers value extra units more than they cost to produce, but the monopolist does not produce them.

explanation: Industry refers to the collection of firms in a market, not to one firm.

option_b: marginal revenue equals average revenue at every output
option_c: the firm is a price taker
option_d: marginal revenue is below average revenue
explanation: To sell one more unit the monopolist lowers the price on all units, so the extra revenue is less than the price. MR lies below AR.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention

option_a: marginal cost is below average variable cost
option_b: price equals minimum average total cost, so profit is normal
option_d: price is above average total cost
explanation: Free entry drives price to the minimum of average total cost. The firm then earns normal profit and is productively efficient.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: In long-run monopolistic competition the firm
option_a: earns normal profit and has excess capacity, producing less than the output at minimum average cost
option_c: sets price equal to marginal cost
option_d: produces at the minimum of average cost
explanation: Entry shifts the firm's demand until it is tangent to average cost, which is normal profit. Tangency is on the falling part of average cost, so there is excess capacity, and price still exceeds marginal cost.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention
stem: In the kinked-demand model of oligopoly, price is rigid because
option_b: rivals are assumed to match a price cut but not a price rise
option_c: demand is perfectly elastic for a price cut
explanation: A price rise loses customers if rivals do not follow, while a price cut is matched so sales hardly rise. The kink creates a break in marginal revenue, and marginal cost can move inside that break without changing price.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Market Structure, Market Failure and Intervention

option_b: price is greater than marginal cost
option_c: the firm holds spare capacity on purpose
explanation: Allocative efficiency requires P = MC, so the value consumers place on the last unit equals the cost of producing it. Perfect competition meets that condition.

option_c: the month of the year only
option_d: the colour of the product only
explanation: Those four features are the usual basis for perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition and oligopoly.

option_b: Many sellers of an identical product and free entry

option_d: A few firms that must each take the price as given
explanation: Monopoly is a single seller protected by barriers, so close substitutes and free entry are absent.

option_a: One seller protected by barriers to entry
option_b: A few interdependent sellers of similar products
option_c: Many buyers and sellers, a homogeneous product, free entry and perfect information
option_d: Many sellers of differentiated products and free entry
explanation: Perfect competition requires price-taking firms selling an identical product, with no barriers to entry.

option_b: barriers stop new firms from entering
explanation: Barriers protect supernormal profit. Free entry, as in perfect or monopolistic competition, competes that profit away in the long run.

option_a: entry of firms, a lower market price, and only normal profit

option_d: exit of firms and a higher price
explanation: Supernormal profit attracts entry. Market supply rises, price falls, and profit is competed down to normal profit.

The firm produces the largest output at which marginal cost does not exceed price, provided price is greater than average variable cost. It should produce
explanation: Marginal cost stays at or below EC$20 up to 3 units and is higher after that. AVC at 3 units is EC$14, which is below price, so the firm covers variable cost.

explanation: Total revenue is EC$30 × 4 = EC$120. Total cost is EC$15 + EC$48 = EC$63. Economic profit is EC$57. At this output AVC is EC$12 and marginal cost of the unit is EC$18.

topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
stem: A Gini coefficient of 0 means
option_b: that the country has no income
option_d: that the Lorenz curve cannot be drawn
explanation: The Gini coefficient runs from 0, perfect equality, toward 1, or 100 if expressed as a percentage, for perfect inequality. This item does not ask for a calculation.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
stem: A means-tested benefit, compared with a universal benefit of the same total cost,
option_a: can concentrate help on low-income households but may discourage extra earnings if the benefit is withdrawn sharply
option_c: is paid to every household regardless of income and therefore always costs less
option_d: is the same thing as a regressive tax
explanation: Means-testing targets the poor. A high withdrawal rate as earnings rise acts like a high marginal tax and can create a poverty trap.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
stem: A poverty line is
option_a: the diagonal of the Lorenz curve
option_b: the income threshold used to decide who is counted as poor
explanation: People below the line are classified as poor. An absolute line is a fixed real basket. A relative line is often a fraction of median income.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
stem: A progressive income tax is one in which
option_a: the average rate of tax rises as income rises
option_b: the average rate of tax is constant
option_c: every household pays the same number of dollars
option_d: the average rate of tax falls as income rises
explanation: Progressive means the average tax rate rises with income. A constant average rate is proportional. A falling average rate is regressive.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
stem: Absolute poverty means
option_b: a person has less income than the richest household
option_c: a person falls below a fixed minimum standard of living
option_d: income is below the national average, even if basic needs are met
explanation: Absolute poverty uses a fixed threshold, such as the cost of a basic basket of food, clothing and shelter. It does not depend on how rich other people are.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
stem: Inequality of opportunity differs from inequality of outcome because
option_b: opportunity is measured only by the terms of trade
option_c: opportunity concerns unequal access to education, jobs or assets, while outcome is the resulting income or wealth
explanation: Two societies can have different views about whether a gap in results is acceptable if the starting chances were equal. The syllabus distinction is between the chances people have and the incomes they end up with.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
stem: On a Lorenz curve, greater inequality is shown by
option_a: a curve lying on the diagonal
option_b: a curve further from the diagonal line of equality
explanation: The diagonal means each share of households receives the same share of income. The further the Lorenz curve bows away, the more unequal the distribution.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
stem: Relative poverty means
option_a: a person is below a threshold that never refers to other people
option_c: the functional share of wages is zero
option_d: a person is poor compared with the typical living standard in that society
explanation: Relative poverty depends on the distribution. A household can meet basic needs and still be relatively poor if its income is far below the median.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
stem: The functional distribution of income shows
option_a: how income is shared among wages, rent, interest and profit
option_d: how income is shared among households
explanation: Functional distribution classifies income by the factor that earns it. Size distribution classifies it by people or households.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
stem: The size distribution of income shows
option_a: how income is shared among individuals or households
option_c: only the share of profit in national income
option_d: export prices relative to import prices
explanation: Size distribution answers who receives income, from richest to poorest, rather than which factor earned it.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
stem: A minimum wage can reduce poverty among workers who keep their jobs, but it may not reduce poverty overall if
option_a: every worker's marginal product rises by the amount of the wage
option_b: the wage is set below equilibrium and does not bind
option_c: employment of low-skilled workers falls and some lose all of their wage
option_d: the labour market is in equilibrium at a wage above the minimum
explanation: The workers who remain employed gain. Workers who become unemployed lose wage income. The net effect on poverty is therefore not guaranteed.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
stem: A sales tax of 10 percent on all goods takes a larger share of a low income than of a high income, because the low-income household spends all of its income. The burden of the tax is
option_a: a poll tax, which is unrelated to spending
explanation: Even a flat rate on spending can be regressive if poorer households spend a larger fraction of income. The average tax rate then falls as income rises.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
stem: Cash transfers to low-income households are intended to
option_a: reduce poverty and narrow the size distribution of disposable income
option_b: raise the Gini coefficient on purpose
explanation: Transfers raise the disposable income of people at the bottom. They are a direct tool of poverty alleviation and redistribution.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
stem: Country A has a Gini coefficient of 0.30 and Country B has a Gini coefficient of 0.55. On this measure,
option_c: income is more unequal in B than in A
option_d: income is more unequal in A than in B
explanation: A higher Gini coefficient means a more unequal size distribution. No formula needs to be evaluated to rank the two figures.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
stem: Public spending on basic education can reduce long-run inequality by
option_c: replacing the Lorenz curve with a demand curve
option_d: raising the human capital and future earnings of children from poor households
explanation: Education is both a merit good and a way of widening access to better-paid work. The effect on inequality is long run, through earning power.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
stem: Regional policy that attracts firms to a poor parish is meant to reduce inequality by
option_a: lowering the marginal product of every worker
option_b: raising labour demand and wages or employment in that parish
option_c: replacing absolute poverty with a higher Gini coefficient on purpose
option_d: shifting the parish's labour demand to the left
explanation: If jobs move to the poor region, local labour demand rises. That can narrow regional income gaps, though it has a cost and may not succeed if firms do not come.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
stem: The share of wages in national income rises and the share of profits falls. This is a change in
option_b: the price elasticity of demand only
explanation: Functional distribution is the split of income among factors. A move from profit toward wages is a change in that split, even before we know how households are affected.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
stem: Which is a recognised cause of poverty in a labour market?
option_a: Prolonged unemployment of the household's earners
option_b: A wage equal to a high marginal revenue product for every worker
option_d: Perfect equality on the Lorenz curve
explanation: Households without work, or with only low-paid work, are more likely to fall below a poverty line. Equality would not itself be a cause of poverty.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
stem: Which outcome is possible?
option_a: A Gini coefficient of 0 means one person has all the income
option_b: The Lorenz curve lies on the diagonal when inequality is extreme
option_c: Functional distribution and size distribution are the same concept
option_d: Absolute poverty falls while relative poverty rises
explanation: Growth can lift people above a fixed poverty line while the gap between rich and poor widens. Absolute and relative poverty therefore need not move together.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: Income Inequality, Poverty and Poverty Alleviation
stem: Which policy is aimed directly at the size distribution of income?
option_b: A devaluation intended only to switch expenditure
option_c: A more progressive income tax combined with transfers
explanation: Tax-and-transfer policy changes disposable incomes across households. The other policies are macroeconomic instruments with different primary targets.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: The Demand for and Supply of Factors
stem: A firm hiring labour in a perfectly competitive labour market should hire extra workers while
option_a: the wage is above marginal revenue product
option_b: marginal revenue product is above the wage, and stop when they are equal
explanation: The wage is the marginal cost of labour to a competitive employer. Profit rises by hiring while MRP exceeds that cost.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: The Demand for and Supply of Factors
stem: A monopsony in a labour market is
option_c: a single seller of the product
explanation: Monopsony power is on the buying side. Monopoly power is on the selling side. A firm can have one without the other.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: The Demand for and Supply of Factors
stem: A profit-maximising monopsonist hires labour where
option_a: marginal cost of labour equals marginal revenue product, and pays the lower wage read from the supply curve
option_b: the wage equals marginal revenue product, as in perfect competition
option_c: marginal cost of labour is below the wage
option_d: employment is higher than under perfect competition
explanation: Because the supply of labour slopes upward, hiring one more worker raises the wage paid to all, so the marginal cost of labour is above the wage. The monopsonist equates that marginal cost with MRP and pays only the supply-curve wage, which is below MRP.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: The Demand for and Supply of Factors
stem: Economic rent is
option_b: the same as normal profit by definition in every market
option_c: payment that is only just enough to keep the factor in its current use
option_d: payment to a factor above its transfer earnings
explanation: Economic rent is a surplus. It can be earned by any factor whose supply is less than perfectly elastic, not only by land.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: The Demand for and Supply of Factors
stem: Marginal revenue product of labour is
option_a: marginal physical product multiplied by marginal revenue
option_c: marginal physical product multiplied by the wage
explanation: MRP is the extra revenue from hiring one more worker. It equals MPP times MR. Only in perfect product-market competition does MR equal price.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: The Demand for and Supply of Factors
stem: Quasi-rent is
option_b: the wage in a perfectly elastic labour market
option_c: economic rent that lasts forever on a factor in permanently fixed supply
option_d: a surplus earned in the short run by a factor whose supply is temporarily fixed
explanation: In the short run some factors cannot leave, so their earnings contain a temporary surplus. In the long run that surplus can be competed away. Permanent rent applies when supply stays fixed.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: The Demand for and Supply of Factors
stem: The demand curve for labour slopes downward, other things equal, because
option_a: the supply of labour is fixed
option_c: diminishing returns reduce marginal physical product as more workers are hired
option_d: transfer earnings rise with the wage automatically
explanation: With other factors fixed, extra workers add less output. MRP therefore falls, and the firm hires more workers only at a lower wage.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: The Demand for and Supply of Factors
stem: The demand for labour is a derived demand because
option_a: labour is demanded for the output it helps to produce, not for its own sake
option_b: the supply of labour slopes upwards
explanation: Firms hire labour only because consumers demand the product. If product demand rises, the demand for the labour that makes it rises.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: The Demand for and Supply of Factors
stem: The reward to enterprise is
explanation: Land receives rent, labour wages, capital interest, and enterprise profit.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: The Demand for and Supply of Factors
stem: The supply of labour to an occupation slopes upward when
option_a: a higher wage always reduces hours because leisure is the only good
option_c: the marginal revenue product is falling
option_d: a higher wage attracts more workers into that occupation
explanation: The substitution toward work, and entry from other occupations, typically make the supply curve of an occupation slope upward. A backward-bending supply of hours for one person is a separate possibility and is not the usual market supply curve.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: The Demand for and Supply of Factors
stem: Transfer earnings of a factor are
option_a: any payment above the minimum needed to keep it in its current use
option_b: a government transfer payment to households
option_c: the minimum payment needed to keep that factor in its current use
option_d: the total wage bill of the industry
explanation: Transfer earnings compensate the factor for not moving to its next best use. Payment above that is economic rent.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: The Demand for and Supply of Factors
stem: Value of the marginal product differs from marginal revenue product when
option_b: the firm sells in perfect competition, so price equals marginal revenue
option_c: the firm sells in an imperfect product market, so marginal revenue is below price
option_d: the wage is equal to MRP
explanation: VMP multiplies marginal product by price. MRP multiplies it by marginal revenue. They coincide only when the product market is perfectly competitive.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: The Demand for and Supply of Factors
stem: A tax that takes part of the economic rent of a factor in perfectly inelastic supply
option_b: does not reduce the quantity supplied of that factor
option_c: shifts a perfectly inelastic supply curve to the left
option_d: is a tax on transfer earnings only
explanation: If the factor is supplied whatever the payment, taxing the surplus does not change the quantity offered. The same tax on transfer earnings could drive the factor away.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: The Demand for and Supply of Factors
stem: An increase in immigration that raises the supply of labour, with demand unchanged, will in a competitive market
option_a: raise the wage and lower employment
option_c: leave both wage and employment unchanged
option_d: lower the equilibrium wage and raise employment
explanation: A rightward shift of labour supply moves the market down the demand curve: a lower wage and higher employment.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: The Demand for and Supply of Factors
stem: Compared with a competitive labour market, a monopsonist tends to
option_b: employ more workers and pay a higher wage
option_d: employ fewer workers and pay a lower wage
explanation: The monopsony outcome is inside the competitive employment level, and the wage is read from supply, below the competitive wage.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: The Demand for and Supply of Factors
stem: Demand for the product made by workers in Golden Vale falls. The demand curve for their labour
option_a: shifts left because marginal revenue product is lower
option_c: is unchanged, because product demand does not affect derived demand
option_d: becomes the supply curve of labour
explanation: Labour demand is derived from product demand. Lower product price or lower sales reduce MRP, so firms hire fewer workers at each wage.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: The Demand for and Supply of Factors
stem: The price of breadfruit rises and workers' physical productivity is unchanged. For a competitive breadfruit farm, the demand for labour
option_a: is unchanged because wages fix MRP
option_c: becomes perfectly inelastic at zero employment
option_d: shifts right because marginal revenue product is higher
explanation: MRP = MPP × price in this product market. A higher product price raises MRP at each employment level, which is a higher demand for labour.

stem: A trade union that raises wages above the competitive equilibrium in an otherwise competitive labour market will
option_a: shift labour demand to the right by the amount of the wage rise
option_b: make the supply of labour perfectly inelastic
option_c: reduce employment in that market if the employer still hires along the demand curve
explanation: A higher wage on a downward-sloping demand curve reduces the quantity of labour demanded, unless the union also raises productivity or the employer is a monopsonist.

option_c: a price-taking labour market on both sides

option_b: a surplus of labour, meaning some workers who want jobs at that wage do not get them

option_d: only reduce employment, as it must in perfect competition
explanation: The minimum wage can become the marginal cost of labour over a range, so the monopsonist hires more workers than at the unrestricted monopsony outcome, up to the competitive employment level.

option_b: a surplus on the current account only

option_b: the demand for money is perfectly elastic at a low interest rate, so increasing the money supply does not lower the rate further

explanation: In a liquidity trap, extra money is held idle. Monetary policy cannot cut the interest rate, so Keynesians look to fiscal policy.

option_c: 0, so the policy has no effect

stem: The paradox of thrift, in a Keynesian model with spare capacity, says that
option_a: consumption and saving move in opposite directions for one household but income is fixed for the economy
option_b: an attempt by everyone to save more can reduce income so that actual saving does not rise
option_c: higher saving always raises equilibrium income
option_d: the interest rate falls and investment rises enough to keep income at full employment
explanation: For one household, saving more is possible if income is given. For the economy, less consumption lowers income, and saving, which depends on income, may not increase.
