stem: A central Classical assumption is that
option_a: the money supply never affects prices
option_b: aggregate demand alone sets real output at every price
option_c: wages, prices and interest rates are flexible and the economy tends to full employment
option_d: wages are stuck, so the economy can stay below full employment indefinitely
explanation: Classical models rely on flexible markets to clear labour, goods and loanable funds at full employment.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: Classical unemployment is viewed mainly as
option_a: voluntary or temporary, because flexible wages clear the labour market
option_b: the same thing as a liquidity trap
option_c: a permanent equilibrium below full employment caused by sticky wages
explanation: If the real wage can fall, the quantity of labour demanded rises until everyone who wants work at that wage is employed. Remaining unemployment is frictional or a choice not to work at the going wage.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: Crowding out, in a Classical full-employment setting with a fixed money supply, means
option_a: taxes automatically fall in a boom
option_b: the multiplier is larger than in a deep recession
option_c: government spending raises private investment dollar for dollar with no interest-rate effect
option_d: government borrowing raises the interest rate and reduces private investment
explanation: At full employment, extra public borrowing competes for funds, the interest rate rises, and private investment falls. The net rise in demand is then smaller.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: In the Classical model, the long-run aggregate supply curve is
option_b: the same curve as aggregate demand
option_d: vertical at the full-employment level of output
explanation: With flexible wages, output is pinned at full employment. A rise in aggregate demand raises the price level rather than real output in the long run.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: Say's Law, as used in the Classical model, says that
option_a: saving always exceeds investment at full employment
option_b: demand creates its own supply with sticky prices
explanation: Producing goods generates the incomes with which those goods are bought, so a general glut of goods is ruled out in the strict Classical story.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: Which contrast is correct?
option_a: Both schools deny that aggregate demand can affect prices
option_b: Classical economists expect flexible wages to restore full employment; Keynesians allow sticky wages and an equilibrium below full employment
option_c: Keynesians assume the interest rate always clears the goods market at full employment
option_d: Classical economists assume a horizontal aggregate supply curve at every output
explanation: The policy difference follows from the assumption about wage and price flexibility. Keynesian under-employment equilibrium is possible when wages do not fall.

stem: A point on the Classical long-run aggregate supply curve shows
option_a: full-employment output, whatever the price level
option_b: unemployment of labour at a sticky wage
explanation: Because the curve is vertical, each price level is associated with the same full-employment output.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: A rightward shift of long-run aggregate supply, in a Classical diagram, can be caused by
option_a: a higher money supply with no change in productive capacity
option_d: growth of the labour force or an improvement in technology
explanation: Long-run supply shifts when potential output changes. A monetary expansion shifts aggregate demand and, in this model, changes prices rather than potential output.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: In the Classical loanable-funds story, a rise in saving
option_a: lowers the interest rate and raises investment until saving and investment are equal
option_b: causes a permanent glut of goods
option_c: raises the interest rate and cuts investment
option_d: has no link to the interest rate
explanation: Flexible interest rates equate planned saving and planned investment. Extra saving pushes the interest rate down and encourages investment.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: In the Classical model, an increase in the money supply, with velocity stable and output at full employment,
option_a: raises real output in proportion and leaves prices unchanged
option_b: raises the price level in proportion
explanation: The quantity theory, MV = PY, with V and Y fixed, implies that P moves in proportion to M.

stem: Investment, in national-income accounting, means
option_b: spending on capital goods, changes in stocks, and new buildings

explanation: Buying an existing financial asset only transfers ownership. Investment in this module is the creation of real capital.

stem: Replacement investment is
option_a: a withdrawal from the circular flow
option_c: the same as net investment by definition
option_d: spending to make good depreciation of the existing capital stock
explanation: Gross investment equals net investment plus replacement of worn-out capital. Net investment is the addition to the capital stock.

stem: The accelerator principle says that net investment depends on
option_a: last year's interest rate only, with output irrelevant
option_c: the rate of change of national income, not only on the level of income
explanation: If firms want a stock of capital in proportion to output, they invest when output is rising. If the growth of output slows, investment can fall even while output is still high.

stem: The marginal efficiency of capital is
option_b: the flow of investment during a year, drawn against the interest rate, including shifts from business confidence
option_c: the expected rate of return on an extra unit of the capital stock
explanation: MEC is a stock concept: the return expected from one more machine. It is compared with the interest rate. MEI is the related flow of investment spending.

stem: The marginal efficiency of investment schedule shifts when
option_b: business confidence, technology or the cost of capital goods changes, at a given interest rate
option_c: only the interest rate changes, moving the economy along the schedule
option_d: the money supply is constant and nothing else happens
explanation: A change in the interest rate is a movement along the MEI schedule. Expectations, technical progress and capital-goods prices shift it.

stem: A firm compares the marginal efficiency of capital with the interest rate. It buys the extra machine if
option_a: the expected rate of return is below the interest rate
option_c: the expected rate of return is above the interest rate
option_d: the interest rate is equal to the wage
explanation: The interest rate is the opportunity cost of funds. A project whose expected return exceeds that cost adds to profit.

option_a: the capital stock must fall to zero

explanation: The accelerator ties investment to the change in output. A smaller increase in output requires a smaller addition to the capital stock, so investment drops.

explanation: Better expectations raise the return at each interest rate, which is a shift. A higher interest rate is a movement up the existing schedule and lower investment.

stem: Disposable income is

explanation: Personal income is received by households. Disposable income is what remains after personal taxes. It is the income behind consumption and saving.

stem: A structural budget deficit is
option_b: the part of the deficit caused only by a recession
option_d: the deficit that would remain even if the economy were at its normal level of output
explanation: The cyclical deficit appears because revenue falls and benefits rise in a downturn. The structural deficit is the underlying stance of the budget.

stem: Automatic stabilisers are
option_a: tax and benefit rules that reduce the amplitude of the business cycle without a new policy decision
option_b: discretionary changes announced in each budget
option_c: tariffs that change every week by ministerial order
explanation: In a boom, income-tax revenue rises and unemployment benefits fall, which withdraws spending. In a slump the opposite happens.

stem: Crowding in occurs when
option_a: public investment raises the profitability of private investment, so private investment rises
option_b: public borrowing necessarily cuts private investment one for one at full employment
explanation: Roads, ports or a more secure outlook can complement private projects. Crowding out is the opposite interest-rate or resource effect.

explanation: The budget is the fiscal instrument. Monetary policy uses the money supply and interest rates.

stem: A government wants to reduce demand-pull inflation. A suitable fiscal action is
option_a: buying securities on the open market, which is fiscal policy
option_c: increasing transfer payments to households by a large amount
option_d: raising taxes or cutting government spending
explanation: Contractionary fiscal policy reduces aggregate demand. Expansion would widen an inflationary gap.

stem: During a boom, income-tax revenue rises and unemployment benefits fall. This automatic change
option_a: raises the multiplier above its recession value
explanation: The budget moves toward surplus, or a smaller deficit, without anyone voting a new tax. That leakage slows the rise in disposable income.

stem: Near full employment, a bond-financed rise in government spending is more likely to crowd out private investment if
option_a: taxes are cut by the same amount and the balanced-budget multiplier is the only effect considered, with interest rates fixed
option_b: the money supply does not rise and the interest rate increases
option_c: the economy is in a liquidity trap
option_d: there is a deep recession and idle saving
explanation: With little spare capacity and a fixed money supply, extra borrowing pushes up interest rates. In a liquidity trap or a deep slump, that channel is weak.

stem: The public-sector borrowing requirement in a year is a
option_c: stock of debt accumulated over all past years
explanation: Borrowing during a year is a flow. The national debt is the stock that results from past borrowing that has not been repaid.

stem: Which is expansionary fiscal policy?
option_a: A rise in income tax rates
option_b: A cut in capital spending with no other change
option_c: A cut in income tax or a rise in government spending on goods and services
explanation: Lower taxes or higher spending raise aggregate demand. Higher taxes or lower spending are contractionary.

stem: Why might fiscal policy act with a lag?
option_a: Tax rates change output on the same morning they are drafted, with no delay
option_b: Automatic stabilisers require a new law every month
option_c: It takes time to recognise the problem, pass a budget and spend the money
option_d: Government spending is not part of aggregate demand
explanation: Recognition, decision and implementation lags mean a stimulus can arrive after the recession has already turned.

explanation: Repos and reverse repos let the central bank add or withdraw reserves for a short period. The repo rate is a policy interest rate.

option_b: the same as the demand for capital goods
option_c: perfectly inelastic at every interest rate, in Keynes's basic account
option_d: inversely related to the rate of interest
explanation: At a high interest rate, bonds are attractive and the opportunity cost of holding money is high, so speculative balances are small. At a low rate, people hold money rather than bonds that may fall in price.

stem: The transactions demand for money rises when

option_d: Medium of exchange, Gini coefficient, terms of trade and tariff

option_b: contractionary, because banks can lend a smaller fraction of deposits

explanation: The simple multiplier assumes banks lend out everything above required reserves and that the public does not drain cash. Excess reserves and a cash drain both reduce the expansion.

explanation: Y = MV/P = 80 × 5 / 2 = 200. PY is nominal output, so output is found by dividing MV by P.

stem: A high debt-service ratio means
option_a: the budget is always in surplus
option_b: the terms of trade equal 100 by definition
option_c: exports are larger than debt service, so the ratio is low
option_d: a large share of export earnings goes to interest and principal on external debt
explanation: Debt service divided by exports shows the foreign-exchange burden. A high ratio leaves less foreign exchange for imports of fuel, food and capital goods.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: The burden of the debt on future generations is clearest when
option_b: debt is external, so future residents must transfer real resources to foreigners
option_c: the government prints a stock of money and calls it debt service without any further consequence
option_d: debt is internal, interest is taxed back from the same residents, and there is no other effect
explanation: External debt service is a real transfer abroad. Internal debt is mainly a transfer among residents, though taxes that pay the interest can still distort incentives.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: The national debt is
option_c: the stock of government borrowing that has not yet been repaid
option_d: the deficit of the current year only
explanation: A deficit is the flow added during the year. The debt is the accumulated stock.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: A budget deficit this year, financed by borrowing,
option_a: is the same statistic as the debt-service ratio
option_b: reduces the national debt by the amount of the deficit
option_c: is a stock, not a flow
explanation: The deficit is new borrowing. Unless it is financed in a way that does not create a liability, the stock of debt rises.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: Inflation reduces the real burden of a domestic debt fixed in money terms if
option_a: the nominal interest rate does not rise fully with inflation
option_b: tax revenue is fixed in nominal terms and spending is indexed
option_c: the debt is indexed to the price level and the real interest rate stays constant
option_d: the debt is denominated in a foreign currency that appreciates
explanation: Unexpected inflation erodes the real value of money debts. If the debt is indexed, or if lenders raise the nominal interest rate fully, that erosion is prevented.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: Internal debt differs from external debt because
option_a: interest on internal debt is paid to residents, whereas external debt service uses foreign currency and is paid to non-residents
option_b: internal debt has no opportunity cost of any kind
option_c: they are both stocks of private company shares
option_d: external debt never has to be serviced
explanation: Internal interest is a transfer inside the country. External service is a leakage of foreign exchange. Both can still displace other public spending.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: Refinancing a loan replaces a maturing debt with a new loan. The debt stock
option_a: need not fall, because one liability replaces another
explanation: Rolling over debt changes its timing or its interest rate. It is not the same as repaying the debt from a surplus.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: Which is a way of reducing the burden of an external debt?
option_a: Borrowing more abroad only to pay interest, with exports unchanged, and calling that a fall in the burden
option_b: Redefining the debt as internal without repaying the foreign creditors
option_d: Earning more foreign exchange through exports, so that the debt-service ratio falls
explanation: A larger export base, concessional refinancing, or faster growth of the capacity to pay can reduce the burden. New borrowing that only rolls up interest does not remove it.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: In Harbour Cay, external interest payments are EC$40 million and principal repayments are EC$20 million. Exports of goods and services are EC$400 million. The debt-service ratio, (interest + principal repayments) / exports × 100, is
explanation: Debt service is 40 + 20 = 60. The ratio is 60/400 × 100 = 15 percent.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

explanation: Debt service is 12 + 8 = 20. The ratio is 20/80 × 100 = 25 percent.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

explanation: Debt service is 45 + 15 = 60. The ratio is 60/300 × 100 = 20 percent.

explanation: Debt service is 30 + 20 = 50. The ratio is 50/200 × 100 = 25 percent.

stem: Cost-push inflation can be started by
option_a: a rise in consumer spending when there is massive spare capacity and no cost increase
option_b: higher import prices, indirect taxes or wage costs that shift aggregate supply to the left
explanation: Higher costs push the price level up and can reduce real output at the same time.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: Demand-pull inflation is caused by
option_a: a fall in the money supply
option_b: a rise in import prices or wages that shifts aggregate supply left
option_d: aggregate demand rising when the economy is near full employment
explanation: Too much spending chasing limited output pulls prices up. Cost-push inflation comes from the supply side.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: Real-wage, or classical, unemployment occurs when
option_a: aggregate demand is high and wages are fully flexible downward
option_b: the real wage is held above the market-clearing level
option_c: workers are between jobs for a week
explanation: If the wage cannot fall, quantity of labour supplied exceeds quantity demanded. That unemployment is not the Keynesian demand-deficient type.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: Stagflation challenged the simple Phillips curve because
option_a: both inflation and unemployment fell to zero
option_c: the curve predicted that outcome exactly and policy never changed
explanation: A supply shock can raise prices and cut output, so unemployment and inflation increase at the same time. That is not a move along a stable downward-sloping Phillips curve.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: The labour force is
option_a: the whole population, including young children
option_c: only people who are not looking for work
option_d: the working-age population minus the employed
explanation: To be unemployed a person must be out of work and actively seeking work, or otherwise meet the survey definition. Others of working age are outside the labour force.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: The natural rate of unemployment is closest to
option_b: frictional plus structural unemployment, with no cyclical unemployment
explanation: Even at 'full' employment, search and mismatch remain. Cyclical unemployment is the part that disappears when demand is strong.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: The short-run Phillips curve shows
option_b: an inverse relationship between unemployment and wage or price inflation
option_c: a positive relationship between unemployment and inflation in every period
explanation: Lower unemployment was associated with higher inflation along the original Phillips curve. The relationship is a short-run trade-off, not a law that holds once expectations adjust.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: Underemployment means
option_a: the labour force has shrunk to zero
option_d: workers are in jobs that use less skill or fewer hours than they want and can offer
explanation: A person can be counted as employed and still be underemployed. The unemployment rate misses that slack. It is sometimes called hidden unemployment when people are not in the measured unemployed.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: A graduate spends six weeks searching for a first job that matches her training. This unemployment is
option_a: seasonal by definition, whatever the month
option_d: the result of a deficiency of aggregate demand lasting several years
explanation: Frictional unemployment is short-term search while moving between jobs or into the labour force. It exists even when there are vacancies.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: A person who has stopped looking for work after many rejections is a discouraged worker. In the standard measure this person is
option_a: in the labour force but not of working age
option_b: unemployed, because they have no job
option_d: outside the labour force, so the unemployment rate does not count them as unemployed
explanation: Discouraged workers are not seeking work, so they are not unemployed. The unemployment rate then understates spare labour.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: A small open island imports most of its fuel. A sharp rise in the world fuel price is most likely to cause
option_b: a fall in the consumer price index in the same month, because imports are excluded
option_c: a deflationary gap with lower prices for sure
explanation: Imported inflation is especially important for Caribbean economies because a large share of consumption and inputs is imported.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: A sugar factory in St Brice closes and the workers' skills are not wanted in tourism. They remain unemployed for a long period. This is mainly
option_a: a fall in the participation rate only, with the workers still counted as employed
option_d: frictional unemployment lasting a few days
explanation: Structural unemployment is a mismatch of skills or location after the pattern of demand or technology changes. It is not cured quickly by a general rise in spending.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: Employment in a fruit-packing plant falls every year after the harvest and recovers next season. This is
option_c: structural unemployment caused by a permanent loss of the industry
explanation: Seasonal unemployment follows a regular calendar pattern in agriculture, tourism or fishing.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: Hotel workers in Harbour Cay lose their jobs because a recession has cut tourist arrivals. This is mainly
option_a: a change in the season that happens every September by custom, with demand otherwise strong
option_c: frictional unemployment caused by normal job search
explanation: Cyclical unemployment rises when aggregate demand falls in a downturn and falls when demand recovers.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: Why might a Caribbean government not rely on a stable Phillips-curve trade-off?
option_a: the island has no labour force
option_b: inflation is defined as a fall in the price level
option_c: unemployment and inflation are the same variable
option_d: Imported inflation and supply shocks can raise prices without reducing unemployment
explanation: If inflation comes from abroad or from domestic costs, cutting demand to slow prices raises unemployment and may not stop the imported part of inflation quickly.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

stem: A managed float means
option_a: the rate is reset only by the IMF each morning for every country
option_b: the rate is permanently fixed and never changes
option_c: the rate is mainly market-determined but the central bank sometimes intervenes
explanation: A managed, or dirty, float sits between a pure float and a hard peg.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: Balance of Payments and Exchange Rates
stem: Devaluation is
option_a: an official increase in the value of a currency
option_c: a market-driven fall in a floating rate
option_d: an official reduction in the value of a currency under a fixed exchange rate
explanation: Depreciation is the market fall under floating rates. Devaluation is the policy step under a peg. Revaluation and appreciation are the upward counterparts.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

topic: Balance of Payments and Exchange Rates
stem: Expenditure-switching policy differs from expenditure-reducing policy because
option_b: both mean a rise in government spending
option_c: switching is a cut in the money supply only
option_d: switching tries to move spending toward home goods, while reducing tries to cut total spending and imports
explanation: Devaluation or depreciation, and tariffs, are switching instruments. Higher taxes or interest rates that cut absorption are reducing instruments.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
topic: Balance of Payments and Exchange Rates
stem: Foreign direct investment is recorded in
option_a: the current account as a good
option_c: the financial account, not the current account
explanation: FDI is a capital flow that buys a lasting stake. It is not an export of a good, so it is not a current-account item.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
topic: Balance of Payments and Exchange Rates
stem: The Marshall-Lerner condition says that a devaluation improves the current account if
option_a: the country has a fixed quantity of exports and imports that cannot change
option_c: the sum of the elasticities is less than 1
option_d: the sum of the price elasticities of demand for exports and imports is greater than 1
explanation: If quantities hardly respond, the fall in export prices worsens the account. Enough elasticity of demand is needed for volumes to offset that price effect.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
topic: Balance of Payments and Exchange Rates
stem: The current account of the balance of payments includes
option_a: trade in goods, trade in services, primary income and secondary income
explanation: Goods and services are the trade balance in the broad sense. Primary income covers investment income. Secondary income covers transfers. FDI belongs in the financial account.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
topic: Balance of Payments and Exchange Rates
stem: Under a fixed exchange rate the central bank
option_a: buys or sells foreign currency to keep the rate at the peg
option_b: lets the rate move to whatever the market sets that day
option_d: sets fiscal policy as its only tool
explanation: Defending a peg uses reserves. If the currency is under downward pressure, the bank sells foreign currency and buys its own.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
topic: Balance of Payments and Exchange Rates
stem: An appreciation of the domestic currency tends to
option_a: make imports dearer and exports cheaper
option_b: make imports cheaper and can reduce imported inflation, while making exports dearer
option_c: raise the foreign-currency price of imports
explanation: A stronger currency buys more foreign goods per unit. Import prices in local currency fall. Exporters find it harder to sell.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
topic: Balance of Payments and Exchange Rates
stem: The EC dollar depreciates under a floating rate. Exports priced in EC dollars become
option_b: cheaper in foreign currency, which can switch spending toward local goods
option_d: a reason to call the change a revaluation
explanation: Foreigners need fewer units of their own currency to buy the exports. That expenditure-switching effect depends on the regime being a float, so the word is depreciation, not devaluation.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
topic: Balance of Payments and Exchange Rates
stem: Under a floating exchange rate, a rise in demand for a country's exports tends to
option_d: leave the rate unchanged because floating rates are fixed by decree
explanation: Foreigners need the local currency to buy the exports, so demand for that currency rises and it appreciates if the rate floats.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: A common market goes beyond a customs union by allowing
option_a: free movement of factors of production among members
option_b: each member to set a different external tariff
option_d: only free movement of goods, with labour and capital still blocked
explanation: Goods, services, labour and capital can move. An economic union goes further and harmonises economic policy.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: A customs union is a free-trade area plus
option_c: no rules on trade with outsiders
option_d: a common currency and a single central bank, and nothing less
explanation: Members liberalise trade among themselves and apply the same tariff to the rest of the world.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: A free-trade area removes tariffs among members and
option_a: requires free movement of labour and a common fiscal policy
option_d: lets each member keep its own tariff against non-members
explanation: The absence of a common external tariff is what separates a free-trade area from a customs union.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: An economic union typically adds, beyond a common market,
option_a: the abolition of the common external tariff
option_b: harmonised economic policies, and sometimes a common currency
explanation: Policy coordination is the extra step. A monetary union, with one currency, is a deeper form.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: The CARICOM Single Market and Economy is intended to
option_a: be a monetary instrument of a single parish council
option_b: set the world price of oil
option_c: deepen integration among members, including freer movement of goods, services, capital and skills
option_d: replace CARICOM with a free-trade area that keeps barriers to factor movement as its goal
explanation: CSME is the deepening of CARICOM beyond a simple trade preference, toward a single market. It is not itself a world-trade institution.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: Trade creation in a customs union is
option_a: the replacement of higher-cost domestic production by lower-cost imports from a partner
option_c: a fall in exports to zero
option_d: the replacement of lower-cost imports from outside the union by higher-cost partner imports
explanation: Trade creation is a gain. Trade diversion, the shift from a cheaper non-member to a dearer member because of the common external tariff, is a possible loss.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: A small member of a customs union may lose if
option_a: trade creation is the only effect and partner costs are lower
option_b: the common external tariff is zero on a good it already imported freely from the partner
option_c: it specialises according to comparative advantage inside a free-trade area with no diversion
explanation: The welfare effect of joining is the balance of creation and diversion, plus any scale or terms-of-trade effects. Diversion can dominate.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: Before a customs union, St Brice imported cement from the cheapest world supplier. After the union it buys dearer cement from a partner because the common external tariff shuts out the world supplier. This is
option_b: a free-trade area with no external tariff
explanation: The union has diverted trade from a lower-cost outsider to a higher-cost insider. That is trade diversion.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: Which sequence moves from shallower to deeper integration?
option_b: Common market, then a free-trade area that reintroduces internal tariffs as a deepening
option_c: Customs union, then separate external tariffs as a deepening
option_d: Free-trade area, customs union, common market, economic union
explanation: Each step adds a commitment: a common external tariff, then factor mobility, then policy harmonisation.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: Brain drain is
option_a: the import of unskilled labour only
option_c: a surplus on the capital account
option_d: a rise in the domestic birth rate of graduates
explanation: When trained workers leave, the sending country loses human capital. Remittances are a partial offset, not a full replacement for the lost skills.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: Economic development is broader than growth because it includes
option_a: only the rise in nominal GDP
option_b: a higher Gini coefficient by definition
option_d: improvements in living standards, such as health and education, and changes in the structure of the economy
explanation: A country can grow and still fail to develop if health, schooling and the quality of jobs do not improve.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: Economic growth means
option_a: a more equal distribution of a fixed output
option_b: any rise in the price level
option_c: an increase in real national output over time
explanation: Growth is a quantity concept, usually measured by the percentage change in real GDP. It is not the same as development.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: Measurable Economic Welfare, as named in this syllabus, is best understood as
option_a: the same statistic as the Gini coefficient
option_d: an adjustment of a national-income measure for welfare-relevant items such as leisure and environmental costs
explanation: The syllabus uses Measurable Economic Welfare for a welfare-adjusted view of national income. Students are not required to compute the adjustment.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: Sustainable development means meeting present needs
option_a: only by maximising this year's nominal GDP
option_b: by using up natural resources as fast as possible
option_c: without any reference to the environment
option_d: without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs
explanation: The standard definition requires the path of development to be one that future generations can continue.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: The Human Development Index combines indicators of
option_a: inflation, unemployment and the budget deficit only
option_b: exports, imports and the exchange rate only
explanation: HDI is not GDP alone. A country can rank higher in income than in human development if health or schooling lags. Calculation of the index is not required.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: A country has high GDP per capita but short schooling and poor health indicators. Its HDI rank is likely to be
option_a: identical to its income rank, because HDI is GDP
option_b: undefined, because education is not in the index
option_c: improved by the poor health indicators
explanation: HDI averages income with health and education. Weak social indicators pull the index down relative to income alone.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: Growth that destroys a coral reef used by a tourism industry may fail the test of sustainable development because
option_a: environmental costs raise Measurable Economic Welfare automatically
option_b: tourism is not part of GDP
option_c: future income from the reef is sacrificed for a present gain
option_d: any rise in real GDP is sustainable by definition
explanation: Sustainability asks whether the activity can continue. Damaging the natural asset that future output depends on fails that test.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: Which is a source of economic growth?
option_b: A larger current-account deficit with no change in productive capacity
option_c: An increase in the capital stock or an improvement in technology
option_d: A rise in the price level with quantities unchanged
explanation: Growth of potential output comes from more or better factors and from technical progress, not from inflation.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: Which is a structural feature of many small island developing states?
option_a: Perfect diversification of exports by definition
option_b: A large internal market that makes trade unimportant
option_d: A narrow export base and high exposure to hurricanes and world prices
explanation: Small populations, limited land, openness and natural hazards make output and export earnings volatile.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: Real GDP in Golden Vale rises from EC$360 million to EC$396 million. The growth rate, (new real GDP − old real GDP) / old real GDP × 100, is
explanation: Growth = (396 − 360) / 360 × 100 = 10 percent. This is a growth rate of real output, not by itself a measure of development.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: Foreign direct investment is distinguished from portfolio investment because FDI
option_a: is recorded entirely on the current account
option_b: involves a lasting interest and a voice in management
option_c: is a short-term holding of bonds or shares with no control
explanation: Portfolio investment does not seek control. A lasting stake with influence over the enterprise is FDI, even though both are financial flows.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: Globalisation refers to
option_a: closer integration of economies through trade, capital, technology and sometimes labour
option_b: a fall in all cross-border flows by definition
explanation: Globalisation is the process, not a single institution. It covers goods, services, finance and ideas.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: The Caribbean Development Bank is
option_a: the central bank of every Caribbean country
option_b: a regional development bank that lends to Caribbean borrowing members
option_d: a private commercial bank with no development mandate
explanation: The CDB is the regional counterpart, focused on Caribbean development finance, not a global trade or monetary institution.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: The International Monetary Fund mainly provides
option_b: a forum whose main product is a cut in tariffs negotiated as trade rounds
option_c: short-term balance-of-payments support and surveillance of macroeconomic policy
option_d: long-term finance for a harbour, as its primary role
explanation: IMF resources are for external financing problems and are often tied to policy conditions. They are not the World Bank's project loans.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: The World Bank's primary role is
option_a: day-to-day pegging of a floating exchange rate
option_b: acting as a country's commercial bank for household deposits
option_d: setting tariff bindings among all members
explanation: The World Bank group lends and advises for development projects and programmes. It is not the WTO and not the IMF.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: The World Trade Organization is mainly concerned with
option_a: the note issue of a single Caribbean state
option_c: rules for international trade and the settlement of trade disputes
option_d: short-term loans to countries with a balance-of-payments crisis
explanation: The WTO is the trade-rules body. The IMF deals with balance-of-payments finance and surveillance. The World Bank finances development.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: A foreign firm buys a 5-day treasury bill and sells it the next week, with no role in any local company. This is
option_b: portfolio investment, not foreign direct investment
option_c: foreign direct investment, because every financial flow is FDI
explanation: There is no lasting control. Treating portfolio flows as FDI would misclassify the financial account.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: A possible benefit of globalisation for a small Caribbean economy is
option_a: the guaranteed disappearance of all external shocks
option_b: the end of any need for foreign exchange
option_d: wider markets and access to foreign capital and technology
explanation: Openness can raise demand for local exports and bring in investment. It does not remove vulnerability to world prices or storms.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: A possible cost of globalisation for a small open economy is
option_a: greater exposure to external shocks and to footloose capital
option_b: an automatic improvement in the terms of trade every year
option_c: a smaller market for every export, by definition
option_d: the inability to import goods that the country cannot produce
explanation: Capital and demand can leave quickly, and a narrow export base transmits world prices into local income. Those are costs to set against the gains from trade and FDI.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: A non-reciprocal trade preference means
option_a: one partner gives easier access and does not require the same concession in return
option_b: a customs union with a common external tariff
option_d: both partners cut every tariff to zero
explanation: Reciprocal agreements exchange concessions. A one-way preference does not require the beneficiary to liberalise in return.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: A tariff is
option_d: a limit on the number of units imported, with no tax
explanation: A tariff raises the domestic price of the import and raises revenue. A quota limits quantity. A subsidy pays domestic producers. An embargo bans trade.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: Comparative advantage, rather than absolute advantage, is the basis for gains from trade because
option_a: a country must be absolutely more productive in every good before it can export
option_c: trade only helps the country that is larger in every industry
option_d: a country gains by specialising in the good with the lower opportunity cost, even if it is less productive in both goods
explanation: Absolute advantage compares output per worker. Comparative advantage compares opportunity cost. Trade can benefit both sides when those opportunity costs differ.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: Free trade can let a country consume
option_a: at a point that violates opportunity cost inside the trading partner as well, by definition
option_b: only inside its production possibility frontier, with no exception
explanation: Specialisation moves production to the frontier. Trade then allows a consumption bundle outside the frontier that would be impossible in isolation.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: International trade is
option_b: the same thing as the national debt
option_c: trade that takes place only inside one parish
option_d: the exchange of goods and services across national borders
explanation: Trade between residents of different countries is international trade. It is recorded in the balance of payments.
source_note: Original classroom item aligned to CAPE Economics syllabus CXC A20/U2/26 (effective for examinations from May–June 2027). Not a CXC past-paper or specimen item. Figures, where used, are fictional.

module_title: Growth, Sustainable Development and Global Relations
stem: The infant-industry argument for protection says that
option_a: protection should last forever even if the industry never becomes efficient
option_b: tariffs lower the price paid by consumers
option_d: temporary protection may let a new industry gain scale and skill until it can compete
explanation: The argument is for temporary help. A risk is that the industry never grows up and the tariff stays, so consumers keep paying higher prices.

stem: Output per worker per day is: Island A produces 8 units of fish or 4 units of yams; Island B produces 6 units of fish or 6 units of yams. Comparative advantage goes to the producer with the lower opportunity cost. Which statement is correct?
option_a: Island B has a comparative advantage in fish because it has the higher opportunity cost
option_b: Opportunity cost of one unit of fish in Island A is 2 units of yams
option_c: Island A has a comparative advantage in fish because its opportunity cost is 0.5 units of yams, lower than 1
option_d: Island A has a comparative advantage in both goods
explanation: Opportunity cost of one fish is 0.5 yams in Island A and 1 yams in Island B. Island A has the comparative advantage in fish. Island B therefore has the comparative advantage in yams.
